# radio-tool

**Flashes firmware -- OpenRTX among it -- onto TYT, Baofeng, Radioddity and other DMR handhelds from Linux**

- **Version recorded:** 0.3.0+git20260829
- **Categories:** `dmr`, `radio-programming`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/v0l/radio_tool>
- **Needs first:** `dfu-util`

## What it does

radio_tool writes firmware to DMR handhelds over USB, in the bootloader mode each radio is started in for an update: TYT's MD-380, MD-390, MD-UV380, MD-UV390, MD-2017, MD-9600, MD-446 and MD-280, Baofeng's DM-1701, DM-1801 and RD-5R, Radioddity's GD-77, Ailunce's HD1 and Yaesu's FT-70DR (upstream's README table). It also wraps a raw firmware image into the vendor's update format (`--wrap`) and unwraps one, prints what a firmware file is for (`--fw-info`), and on TYT radios reads and sets the clock. OpenRTX, the open firmware with M17 support, names it as the Linux way to put OpenRTX on these radios and to put the original firmware back.
**It writes firmware to the radio.** `--flash` replaces the program the radio runs; an image for the wrong model, or a flash interrupted part way, can leave the radio unable to start until it is flashed again. Installing it changes nothing on any radio, and no firmware comes with it -- OpenRTX's and the manufacturers' images are downloaded by you.

## Why you would want it

The manufacturers' update tools run on Windows. On Linux, `qdmr` and `dmrconfig` (in the catalog) write a radio's codeplug -- its channels and contacts -- but not its firmware; `dfu-util` writes raw DFU images and has no notion of the vendors' wrapped update files. radio_tool is the piece that flashes, and the one OpenRTX's documentation points Linux users at.

## Before it will work

The radio's programming cable, and the radio started in its firmware update mode: OpenRTX's user guide says PTT and the side button above it held while switching on for the MD-3x0 radios, the two side buttons below PTT for the GD-77 family, and the red button with P1 for the MD-9600. The account needs access to the raw USB device. A TYT radio in that mode is an STM32 bootloader (0483:df11), and access to it comes from the udev rule the archive's `dfu-util` ships, which this unit installs as a dependency; the `dmr-radio` hardware class records that pair as a firmware target only, never as a rule matched to whatever is attached (D-028). The RD-5R and GD-77 bootloader (15a2:0073) is an identifier the same class carries, for `dialout`. A firmware image for that exact model, and a codeplug backup first, as OpenRTX's guide says.

## Install and launch

- **Installed by name only** — it is in no profile.
- **Install:** `hammunition install radio-tool --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Commands it leaves on your PATH: `radio_tool`.
- **The install needs the network to:** the upstream files the plan lists, each checked against a pinned digest (or, for map and reference data, the publisher or a LAN mirror).

## Known problems

**List before you flash.** `radio_tool -l` lists the radios it can see with an index; `-d <index>` picks one. Codeplug upload is not supported for these radios (upstream's README table); use `qdmr` or `dmrconfig` for channels. This build has no Bluetooth LE, so `--ble` and `--list-ble`, which upstream added for cloning the Baofeng UV-17Pro family's codeplugs, do nothing useful here; the help still lists them. The README's `--list-radios` is not an option at this commit.
What was measured: built on Debian 13 and Kali, and `radio_tool --help` printed its options ("radio_tool v0.3.0-f9083b6"). `-l` was not run, because it enumerates the USB devices attached. Not measured: any radio, a firmware file, `--wrap`, or a flash.

## Keeping it current

- probe: github tags (`v0l/radio_tool`)
- strategy: rebuild
- Tags are rare (v0.2.2 in 2022, v0.3.0 in 2025) and the 2026-08 fixes are untagged. When a tag lands at or after f9083b6, move to the tag and drop the pin_review; until then read the default branch's head (D-032) at each review. Keep -DBUILD_BLE=OFF unless SimpleBLE can be pinned.
